$T:(u,v,w)\to (x(u,v,w),y(u,v,w),z(u,v,w)).$ The inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}(x,y,z)\to (u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x} \\ \sqrt{y}+z \\ {y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x\ne 0$ and $y>0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{x},\,y(x,y,z)=\sqrt{y}+z,\,z(x,y,z)={y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =0 \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & =1 \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2y & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 0 & 2y & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}|\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} & 1 \\ 2y & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}} & =(\frac{1}{x})^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{{y}^{2}} \\  & ={u}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{w} \\  & =2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{u}^{2}\sqrt{w}}.\end{aligned}

(u(x,y,z),v(x,y,z),w(x,y,z))$ is given by

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}y{z}^{2} \\ z{x}^{2} \\ x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the Jacobian determinant of $T.$

*Hint: You can assume that $x,y,z\ne 0.$*" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we're only given ${T}^{-1}.$ So, we compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)},$ the Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}.$

- Then, we will compute the Jacobian determinant of $T$ using the relation

$$
\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1}.
$$

Here, we have 

$$
u(x,y,z)=y{z}^{2},\,v(x,y,z)=z{x}^{2},\,w(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & =0 & \,\frac{∂u}{∂y} & ={z}^{2} & \,\frac{∂u}{∂z} & =2yz \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & =2xz & \,\frac{∂v}{∂y} & =0 & \,\frac{∂v}{∂z} & ={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & ={y}^{2} & \,\frac{∂w}{∂y} & =2xy & \,\frac{∂w}{∂z} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant of ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} & \frac{∂u}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y} & \frac{∂v}{∂z} \\ \frac{∂w}{∂x} & \frac{∂w}{∂y} & \frac{∂w}{∂z}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & {z}^{2} & 2yz \\ 2xz & 0 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{z}^{2}|\begin{aligned}2xy & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 0\end{aligned}|+2yz|\begin{aligned}2xz & 0 \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{z}^{2}(0-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})+2yz(4{x}^{2}yz-0) \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+8{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} \\  & =9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down $\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)}$ in terms of $u,$ $v,$ and $w,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2} & =9{({x}^{3}{y}^{3}{z}^{3})}^{2/3} \\  & =9{(y{z}^{2}\cdot z{x}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2})}^{2/3} \\  & =9(uvw)^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & ={(\frac{∂(u,v,w)}{∂(x,y,z)})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{9(uvw)^{2/3}}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129270 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128847 :question/id #uuid "b16845a2-5f66-524a-90ea-37f8a8186f8f" :question/math-academy-id "e-11518"} :knowledge-point/id :question/problem "Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-v \\ {u}^{2}+v \\ {e}^{w}\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-v,\,y(u,v,w)={u}^{2}+v,\,z(u,v,w)={e}^{w}.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & ={e}^{w}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 & 0 \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {e}^{w}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{w}|\begin{aligned}2u & -1 \\ 2u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{w}(2u+2u) \\  & =4u{e}^{w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 4u{e}^{w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane."} {:db/id 17592186281338 :question/id #uuid "d47d2404-bd86-5706-ba43-4f015172617a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161809"} {:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d8ced6e6-4bb6-52e9-8819-7a54180e8a4f" :step/math-academy-id 43046 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130234}} {:db/id 17592186130213 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129271 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128848 :question/id #uuid "66d757d2-f2ad-5f0d-b4f1-8d426f4c8351" :question/math-academy-id "e-11579"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d433063f-f145-5bf4-8bd4-8d5e5b36b3d8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048219} {:db/id 17592186048505} {:db/id 17592186049159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129727} {:db/id 17592186129750} {:db/id 17592186281325} {:db/id 17592186281326} {:db/id 17592186281327} {:db/id 17592186281328} {:db/id 17592186406772}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Jacobian of a Three-Dimensional Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "d3c03e1b-973d-566a-96d2-32f746decf45" :step/math-academy-id 43048 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130229}} {:db/id 17592186130229 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130463 :tutorial/content "The **critical points** of a transformation $\mathbf T: \mathbb R^3\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$ given by

![](images/0f/0f47dfd79a5147b5628975b26ea21a37288d809fb30a5a90b205ecc7b25ae008.svg)

are the points in Cartesian $uvw$-space where the Jacobian is zero:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)}=0
$$

  

Similar to the two-dimensional case, the transformation $\mathbf T$ is locally non-invertible at the critical points.

Finally, provided that $\mathbf{T}$ is invertible, the connection between the Jacobians of $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf{T}^{-1}$ is as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\partial (u, v, w)}{\partial (x, y, z)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (x, y, z)}{\partial (u, v, w)} \right)^{-1}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9dd5b9bc-94c3-5fd0-8752-3fa9be521934" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7676 :tutorial/title "The Critical Points of a Transformation"} :step/id #uuid "99520515-6bfa-5265-8e42-e193dc1183f6" :step/math-academy-id 44587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130211}} {:db/id 17592186130234 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130467 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant of a spatial transformation can be interpreted similarly to the Jacobian of a plane transformation.

As before, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

Given that $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ denotes the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0, w_0),$ let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space whose bottom, back left corner is at the point $(u_0,v_0,w_0).$

![](images/31/31c0a7275acdac0dc217e73f3c1e3d9efe504832419c87486cee980e20ea04da.png)

 

It can be shown that, provided that our prism is very small and $(u_0,v_0, w_0)$ is not a critical point of $\mathbf T,$ the image of our prism can be approximated by a parallelepiped. 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangular prism and its (approximate) image:

- The local *volume* scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length, width, and height of our rectangular prism are $\delta u,$ $\delta v,$ and $\delta w,$ so its volume is 

$$
\delta V = \delta u \delta v \delta w.
$$

 Then, it can be shown that the approximate parallelepiped in $xyz$-space has a volume equal to 

$$
\left|J(u_0,v_0,w_0)\right| \cdot \delta V,
$$

 as depicted below.

![](images/d6/d669cd5369d33e618ab43cfd3e93ee70c9fea8420b5a829d78826c11524511aa.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) > 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving. 

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the same orientation (right-handed $\to$ right-handed or left-handed $\to$ left-handed).

![](images/f0/f05f9a79d9156518e948c46f6c67eb5ff31132fd4a088e14219eada7eb49a441.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0, w_0) < 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the opposite orientation (right-handed $\to$ left-handed or left-handed $\to$ right-handed).

![](images/45/45b08e0fec7114db52a05cb42ed46d7d62baa5b01a5dea37752928348802b205.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) \neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a three-dimensional region (i.e., a parallelepiped).

![](images/61/61557eb2d78d468946375b918ab182da518b7cf2c68a1c0a0593c93b991bcf78.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a two-dimensional region (a parallelogram), a one-dimensional region (a line segment), or a zero-dimensional region (a point).

{:db/id 17592186130457 :tutorial/content "Similar to transformations in the plane, we can also consider transformations of three-dimensional regions.

For example, the transformation

![](images/71/71b4c6b8f2db4890436050206115b94eb57b088be76049cb32667f02986b4f56.svg) 

maps a rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space onto one-eighth of a sphere in Cartesian $xyz$-space, as shown below.

![](images/3e/3e1ee5a6116d57cc1c3419b55bf0a9701b9f5d4d93931d053ed4a05b83a5d8f0.png)

 

In general, if a transformation

![](images/d1/d175f9eba3a6da7cc7750b3e59fe0e5904df27511a6b64481598e0f0ebfa1f0c.svg) 

is a $C^1$ transformation, meaning that it and its first derivatives are continuous, then the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, to compute the Jacobian determinant of our transformation above, we first calculate the required partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡v & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v|\begin{aligned}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}|+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w & -u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡w & u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\operatorname{cos}⁡w\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot {u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w)+u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot u{sin}^{2}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡w+{sin}^{2}⁡w) \\  & ={u}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v+{u}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡v\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot ({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v) \\  & ={u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's get some practice at computing Jacobians of three-dimensional transformations." :tutorial/id #uuid "610a6348-ed80-507a-b390-560e9bc1e4ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7237 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186130234 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130467 :tutorial/content "The Jacobian determinant of a spatial transformation can be interpreted similarly to the Jacobian of a plane transformation.

As before, the Jacobian describes *local* effects, not global ones. 

Given that $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ denotes the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf{T}$ evaluated at $(u_0, v_0, w_0),$ let's describe $\mathbf T$'s effect on a *tiny* rectangular prism in Cartesian $uvw$-space whose bottom, back left corner is at the point $(u_0,v_0,w_0).$

![](images/31/31c0a7275acdac0dc217e73f3c1e3d9efe504832419c87486cee980e20ea04da.png)

 

It can be shown that, provided that our prism is very small and $(u_0,v_0, w_0)$ is not a critical point of $\mathbf T,$ the image of our prism can be approximated by a parallelepiped. 

The Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T$ evaluated at $(u_0,v_0,w_0)$ describes the following key features between our tiny rectangular prism and its (approximate) image:

- The local *volume* scale factor of $\mathbf T$. 

Suppose the length, width, and height of our rectangular prism are $\delta u,$ $\delta v,$ and $\delta w,$ so its volume is 

$$
\delta V = \delta u \delta v \delta w.
$$

 Then, it can be shown that the approximate parallelepiped in $xyz$-space has a volume equal to 

$$
\left|J(u_0,v_0,w_0)\right| \cdot \delta V,
$$

 as depicted below.

![](images/d6/d669cd5369d33e618ab43cfd3e93ee70c9fea8420b5a829d78826c11524511aa.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* orientation-preserving or *locally* orientation-reversing.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) > 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving. 

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the same orientation (right-handed $\to$ right-handed or left-handed $\to$ left-handed).

![](images/f0/f05f9a79d9156518e948c46f6c67eb5ff31132fd4a088e14219eada7eb49a441.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0, w_0) < 0,$ the transformation is (locally) orientation-reversing.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps a triple of vectors onto a triple with the opposite orientation (right-handed $\to$ left-handed or left-handed $\to$ right-handed).

![](images/45/45b08e0fec7114db52a05cb42ed46d7d62baa5b01a5dea37752928348802b205.png)

- Whether the transformation is *locally* invertible or *locally* non-invertible.

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0) \neq 0,$ the transformation is (locally) invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a three-dimensional region (i.e., a parallelepiped).

![](images/61/61557eb2d78d468946375b918ab182da518b7cf2c68a1c0a0593c93b991bcf78.png)

 

If $J(u_0,v_0,w_0)= 0,$ the transformation is (locally) non-invertible.

Geometrically, this means that the transformation maps our tiny rectangular prism (a three-dimensional region) onto a two-dimensional region (a parallelogram), a one-dimensional region (a line segment), or a zero-dimensional region (a point).

![](images/0f/0f47dfd79a5147b5628975b26ea21a37288d809fb30a5a90b205ecc7b25ae008.svg)

The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis.
